intro: Built from your own quant mocks. Sections are sorted by your accuracy on their concepts, weakest first, and the numbers update after every finished mock. Each section has the facts to know cold, the shortcuts, and the traps the mocks are built around. Open **Your misses** to reread the full explanation of each question you got wrong.

quickRef.title: Circles & triangles
lines: Circle: $C=2\pi r$, $A=\pi r^2$; arc $=\frac{\theta}{360}\cdot2\pi r$, sector $=\frac{\theta}{360}\cdot\pi r^2$
Square in circle: diagonal $=2r$, area $=2r^2$ · circle in square: side $=2r$
Square in semicircle (side on the diameter): $s^2=\frac45r^2$
Chord $c$ at distance $d$ from the center: $\left(\frac c2\right)^2+d^2=r^2$

quickRef.title: Polygons, solids, coordinates
lines: Slope $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$; $Ax+By=C$ has slope $-\frac AB$ · perpendicular: $m_1m_2=-1$
Distance $\sqrt{\Delta x^2+\Delta y^2}$ · midpoint = average of the coordinates

quickRef.title: Counting, probability, sets
lines: Together: block it, then $\times$ internal orders · apart: total $-$ together

quickRef.title: Number theory & algebra
lines: Odd$^2$ leaves remainder 1 on division by 8 · $k\equiv-1$: even powers $\equiv1$

quickRef.title: Percent, growth, statistics
lines: Equal growth over $k$ periods: each period is the $k$-th root of the total factor
$+c$ to every value: mean, median shift; SD, range don't · $\times k$: all scale by $|k|$

formats.title: Quantitative Comparison
rules: Both quantities fixed numbers? Then (D) is impossible: compute and compare.
With a variable, try the special values: $0$, $1$, $-1$, a fraction between 0 and 1, a negative, a large number, and **both ends** of any range.
One case gives A and another gives B? Stop: it's (D).
Simplify both sides with the same operation; only multiply or divide by something you know is positive.
Figure not to scale: deform it in every way the given facts allow.

formats.title: Multiple choice, one answer
rules: Glance at the choices first: their spread says how precise you need to be, and their form ($\sqrt3$, $\pi$, fractions) hints at the method.
Back-solve from the middle choice when the setup is slow and the question asks for one number.
Pick numbers for questions about variables or percents with no values given.
Wrong choices are the classic slips (half-angle, wrong base, missing $\frac12$). Landing on a choice isn't proof; sanity-check it.

formats.title: Select all that apply
rules: No partial credit: treat every choice as its own true/false question.
First find the general rule (a range, a form like $47k$, the odd numbers from 5 to 65), then test each choice against it and check **both** ends.
Selecting every choice is rarely right. If you're about to, look for the condition built to rule one out: a boundary, 'distinct', 'positive', 'must be'.

formats.title: Numeric Entry
rules: No choices to catch a mistake: reread the last line and **circle the noun** before you type.
Plug your answer back into the original conditions; it takes 15 seconds.
Fractions don't need reducing; decimals need exactly the rounding asked for. Negative answers are allowed.

formats.title: Data Interpretation
rules: Read the title, axes, units and footnotes before the first question; every question in the set shares the figure.
Estimate first; compute only as precisely as the gaps between choices need.
Watch the base of every percent: it changes from question to question.

pacing: The real GRE gives 21 minutes for 12 questions, then 26 minutes for 15: about **1:45** per question.
First pass: answer everything you can in under 2 minutes. At **2:30** with no clear path, mark it, guess, and move on.
Second pass: return to the marked questions with the time you saved. A fresh look often finds the shortcut.
Take the next mocks in **exam mode with the timer on**; untimed accuracy is a ceiling, not your score.
A 170 allows roughly 0–2 misses. The cheapest points to win back are QC traps and misread questions.

sections.title: Circles & inscribed figures
facts: A square inscribed in a circle has its **diagonal** equal to the diameter: $s\sqrt2=2r$, so its area is $2r^2$.
A circle inscribed in a square has diameter equal to the **side**: $s=2r$. In 'square in circle in square' the areas go $4r^2\to\pi r^2\to2r^2$: each square is half the next one out.

Square in a semicircle with one side on the diameter: the square is centered, so a top corner sits at $\left(\frac s2,\,s\right)$ from the center. Then $\left(\frac s2\right)^2+s^2=r^2$ and $s^2=\frac45r^2$.
The perpendicular from the center to a chord **bisects** the chord. Half-chord, center distance and radius make a right triangle: $\left(\frac c2\right)^2+d^2=r^2$.
Arc length $=\frac{\theta}{360}\cdot2\pi r$ uses the **central** angle. An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
tricks: Draw the radius to every point that lies on the circle. Almost every inscribed-figure problem becomes a right triangle with the radius as its hypotenuse.
Put the center at the origin and write a corner's coordinates; $x^2+y^2=r^2$ is then one equation.
Half-chord over radius gives the **half**-angle: $\frac{3\sqrt3}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ means $60^\circ$, so the central angle is $120^\circ$.
Two parallel chords on opposite sides of the center: their distances from the center **add** to the gap between them. On the same side, they subtract.
traps: Using the diameter (or radius) as the inscribed square's side, instead of matching the square's **diagonal** to the diameter.
Taking the half-angle from the half-chord triangle as the central angle: the arc comes out half as long.
Assuming half a circle holds 'half the square'. The semicircle square is $\frac45r^2$, not $r^2$.
Using full chord lengths in the Pythagorean step; it's always the half-chord.

sections.title: Triangles & special right triangles
facts: $45$-$45$-$90$: sides $1:1:\sqrt2$. $30$-$60$-$90$: sides $1:\sqrt3:2$, with the short leg opposite $30^\circ$.

Area $=\frac12bh$ with **any** side as the base, so the altitude to side $a$ is $\frac{2A}{a}$. The 13-14-15 triangle splits into 5-12-13 and 9-12-15, so its area is 84 and its altitudes are 12 (to 14), $\frac{56}{5}$ (to 15) and $\frac{168}{13}$ (to 13).
Triangle inequality: $|a-b|<c<a+b$. An isosceles triangle with legs 5 can have any base strictly between 0 and 10.
The larger angle faces the longer side. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
Similar triangles: lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.
tricks: A non-right triangle with two known angles? **Drop an altitude** from the third vertex so each piece is a special triangle. Angles of $45^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ give a 45-45-90 and a 30-60-90 sharing the altitude.
'Not drawn to scale' means trust only the text. In QC, try to **stretch** the figure: if a length or angle can move while every given fact still holds, the answer is often (D).
Know the triples and their multiples on sight (6-8-10, 9-12-15, 10-24-26) to skip square roots.
traps: Treating a triangle as right-angled because it looks it, or because special angles appear in it.
Using a memorized number (the famous altitude 12) without checking which side it goes to.
Reading a drawn segment as an altitude, bisector or midpoint when nothing says so.
Dropping the $\frac12$ in the area formula.

sections.title: Coordinate geometry
facts: Slope $m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$. The line $Ax+By=C$ has slope $-\frac AB$.
Perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$: flip the sign **and** take the reciprocal ($\frac34\to-\frac43$). Parallel lines share a slope.
Distance $\sqrt{\Delta x^2+\Delta y^2}$; midpoint = average of the coordinates.
$x$-intercept: set $y=0$. $y$-intercept: set $x=0$.
$y=a(x-h)^2+k$ has its vertex at $(h,k)$ and opens up when $a>0$.
$f(x-h)$ shifts right by $h$; $f(x)+k$ shifts up by $k$; $-f(x)$ reflects over the $x$-axis.
tricks: A square from two opposite vertices: the other diagonal has the same midpoint, the same length, and is perpendicular. Take the vector $(a,b)$ from the midpoint to one vertex and rotate it to $(-b,a)$ and $(b,-a)$.
Sketch the points. Choices on the wrong side of an axis, or far too long, go in seconds.
traps: Flipping the sign without taking the reciprocal, or the reverse.
Answering with the $y$-intercept when the $x$-intercept was asked.
Completing a rectangle with horizontal and vertical sides and calling it a square without checking that the sides are equal.

sections.title: Polygons, area & volume
facts: Interior angle sum $(n-2)\cdot180^\circ$; exterior angles always sum to $360^\circ$. Regular polygon: exterior $\frac{360}{n}$, interior $180-\frac{360}{n}$.
Number of diagonals $=\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$.
Fixed perimeter: the square has the largest area. Fixed diagonal $d$: the perimeter can be anything in $(2d,\,2\sqrt2\,d]$, with the square at the top.
Trapezoid $\frac{b_1+b_2}{2}h$; parallelogram $bh$; rhombus $\frac{d_1d_2}{2}$.
Box: $V=lwh$, surface $2(lw+lh+wh)$, space diagonal $\sqrt{l^2+w^2+h^2}$. Cylinder: $V=\pi r^2h$, surface $2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
tricks: Interior is $k$ times exterior? Use interior + exterior $=180^\circ$: exterior $=\frac{180}{k+1}$, then $n=\frac{360}{\text{exterior}}$.
For 'which could be' questions about perimeter or area, find the **range** first (both extremes), then check each choice against it.
With $a^2+b^2=d^2$ fixed, $(a+b)^2=d^2+2ab$, so $a+b$ is largest when $ab$ is: at $a=b$.
traps: Assuming whole-number sides when nothing says so.
Thinking a longer, thinner rectangle has a larger perimeter. With the diagonal fixed it gets **smaller**.
Entering the number of sides when the question asked for diagonals, or forgetting to halve $n(n-3)$.

sections.title: Counting & probability
facts: Order matters: $\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$. Order doesn't: $\binom nk$.
Arrangements with repeats: $\frac{n!}{a!\,b!\cdots}$. AABBCC has $\frac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!}=90$.
Must be together: glue them into one block, arrange the $n-1$ units, then multiply by the block's internal orders ($2!$ for a pair).
Must be apart: total minus together.
Inclusion–exclusion: $|A\cup B\cup C|=\Sigma|A|-\Sigma|A\cap B|+|A\cap B\cap C|$. 'None of the bad things happen' = total minus that.
$P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$; independent: $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)P(B)$; conditional: $P(A|B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$.
tricks: **Place the restricted people first.** Someone who can't sit at either end of 8 seats has 6 choices before anyone else is seated.
When one choice changes how many options the next has, split into cases or count the complement.
Two people not adjacent among $k$ allowed seats in a row: ordered pairs $k(k-1)$ minus adjacent ordered pairs $2(k-1)$. With $k=6$: $30-10=20$.
'Digits in decreasing order', or any forced order, means you only choose a **set**: each set gives exactly one arrangement, so count with $\binom nk$.
Doubt a formula? Shrink the problem to 3 or 4 objects, list them all, and check.
traps: Multiplying choices as if independent when a restriction links them (where Bob can sit depends on where Ann sat).
Forgetting that the two people inside a block can swap.
Stopping inclusion–exclusion early: subtract the singles, add back the pairs, **subtract** the triple.
Halving to get 'even' when even and odd outcomes aren't equally likely.

sections.title: Overlapping sets & min/max
facts: Two sets: $T=A+B-\text{Both}+\text{Neither}$.
Exactly one $=A+B-2\cdot\text{Both}$; at least one $=A+B-\text{Both}$.
Both is bounded: $\max(0,\,A+B-T)\le\text{Both}\le\min(A,B)$.
Three sets: $T=A+B+C-(\text{pair overlaps})+\text{all three}+\text{neither}$, where each pair overlap includes the triple.
tricks: Turn every min/max set question into the bounds on Both. Max 'exactly one' needs the **least** Both; min 'exactly one' needs the most.
For 'which could be', write the quantity as a formula in Both (e.g. $95-2b$), find $b$'s range, then note the step (here: odd numbers only).
Four groups? Draw a 2×2 table (A / not A by B / not B) with totals on the edges.
Min/max in general: push everything else to an extreme. To make one item as large as possible, make the others as small as the constraints allow.
traps: Assuming no overlap, or no 'neither', when the total doesn't allow it.
Checking only parity and forgetting the ends of the range.
Assuming everyone is in at least one set.

sections.title: Number theory
facts: Remainders survive adding and multiplying: replace the base by its remainder first. If $k\equiv-1$ then even powers of $k$ leave 1 and odd powers leave $-1$.
Every odd square leaves remainder 1 on division by 8.
Units-digit cycles: 2, 3, 7, 8 repeat every 4; 4 and 9 every 2; 0, 1, 5, 6 never change.
Each base has its **own** cycle length for a given divisor. List powers until the remainder comes back to 1.
$\gcd(a,b)\cdot\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=ab$. Perfect squares are the only numbers with an odd number of divisors.
$a^ma^n=a^{m+n}$, $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$, $a^{-n}=\frac1{a^n}$. Combine only like bases or like exponents.
tricks: Power remainder: write the first few remainders until they repeat, then reduce the exponent modulo the cycle length.
A remainder condition with a variable: pick the smallest number that fits (remainder 5 on division by 6: $k=5$), then confirm with a second one ($k=11$).
Divisor-count QCs: test $n=1$, a prime, a prime power **and** a product of three primes. The ratio changes with how many primes there are.
traps: Assuming two bases share a cycle length.
Testing only primes or prime powers and missing the case that flips the comparison.
Hunting for a cycle of 4 when the real cycle is 2 or 1.

sections.title: Algebra & inequalities
facts: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative **flips** it. Strict endpoints ($<$) are excluded, so plugging them in proves nothing.

$|x-a|$ is the distance from $x$ to $a$. $|x-a|+|x-b|$ equals $|a-b|$ between the two points and grows by 2 per unit outside them, so $|x-a|+|x-b|\le c$ is the interval $\left[\frac{a+b-c}{2},\,\frac{a+b+c}{2}\right]$.
If $x+\frac1x=s$: $x^2+\frac1{x^2}=s^2-2$, $x^3+\frac1{x^3}=s^3-3s$, $\left(x-\frac1x\right)^2=s^2-4$.
$x^2+bx+c=0$ with roots $r,s$: $r+s=-b$ and $rs=c$. 'Two different roots' rules out the double root.
Two linear equations: one solution when the slopes differ; **none** when the coefficients are proportional but the constants aren't; **infinitely many** when everything is proportional.
Composition $f(g(x))$: work from the inside out.
tricks: Two inequalities: solve each, write the overlap as one interval, then factor the comparison ($x^2+4x=x(x+4)$) and read its sign on that interval.
When a parameter comes out as $k^2=\ldots$, plug **both** roots back into the original.
'Must be an integer' options: compute what the given allows ($s^2-2$, $s^3-3s$); the difference forms usually hide a square root.
Absolute values: mark the points on a number line and read the distances.
traps: Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative.
Counting an excluded endpoint as part of the range.
Choosing the parameter that makes the lines identical (infinitely many solutions) when 'no solution' was asked.
Taking $k=+(r+s)$ instead of $-(r+s)$.

sections.title: Ratios, percent & word problems
facts: Ratio $a:b$ means the parts are $ak$ and $bk$, so the total is a multiple of $a+b$.
Chain ratios through the shared term: $4:7$ and $3:2$ (sharing the 7 and the 3) become $12:21:14$, using the LCM of 7 and 3.
'Percent greater than $X$' $=\frac{\text{difference}}{X}$: the base is the number after 'than'.
An increase of $p\%$ multiplies by $1+\frac p{100}$: $+700\%$ is $\times8$, $-25\%$ is $\times0.75$.
Equal growth each period: the total factor splits by **roots**, not division. $\times8$ over 3 equal blocks is $\times2$ per block.
Rate $\times$ time = work; rates of people working together add: $\frac1a+\frac1b$ per hour.
Simple interest $Prt$; compound $P(1+r)^t$.
tricks: Find what **doesn't change** (the members who don't join, the salt in a mixture) and anchor the equation to it.
Name one variable for the smallest share and write everything else in terms of it.
Before you answer, reread the last line and **circle the noun**: the total, one share, the original or the new amount.
Plug the answer back into the story: 15 seconds that catch most numeric-entry slips.
traps: Entering an intermediate quantity (one person's share, the new total) instead of what was asked.
Combining ratios without a common middle term.
Splitting a compound percent change evenly across periods.
Using the wrong base for 'percent greater', or reporting the ratio (136%) instead of the increase (36%).

sections.title: Data & statistics
facts: The combined mean of groups is **weighted** by group size: $\frac{n_1\bar x_1+n_2\bar x_2}{n_1+n_2}$. It equals the plain average of the means only when the sizes are equal.
Normal: 68% within $1\sigma$, 95% within $2\sigma$. So about 16% lie above $\mu+\sigma$ and about 2.5% above $\mu+2\sigma$.
Quartiles of an even-sized list: Q1 and Q3 are the medians of the lower and upper halves. IQR $=$ Q3 $-$ Q1.
Adding values at the extremes shifts which values sit at the quartile positions, so the IQR can change even though no middle value moved.
Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean and median but not the SD or range. Multiplying by $k$ scales all of them by $|k|$.
SD measures spread around the mean: adding a value equal to the mean shrinks it; adding values far from the mean grows it.
tricks: Several groups and one cutoff: convert the cutoff to a $z$-score **for each group separately** before using 16% or 2.5%.
Data interpretation: estimate first and compute only as precisely as the gaps between the choices need.
Say the units and what each axis or column measures before computing; most DI misses are a misread label, not arithmetic.
traps: Averaging group means without weighting by size.
Using the same tail percentage for groups with different SDs.
Using both tails (32%) when only one tail was asked.
Assuming the IQR can't change when values are added at the ends.

sections.title: QC number sense
facts: $0.\overline{ab}=\frac{ab}{99}$, and $0.\overline{9}=1$ exactly.
For $0<x<1$: $x^2<x<\sqrt x$ and $\frac1x>1$. For $x>1$ the order reverses.
Scientific notation: $0.00052=5.2\times10^{-4}$. Move the decimal and track the exponent.
tricks: Test **at least two very different values**: near each end of the allowed range, plus the special ones ($0$, $1$, $-1$, a fraction, a negative, a large number).
Mismatched results across cases means (D). Stop computing.
Simplify both quantities with the same operation until the comparison is obvious; never multiply by something whose sign you don't know.
traps: Testing a single 'nice' value (like $\frac12$) and calling it.
Believing $0.999\ldots$ is a little less than 1.
Answering a QC with a variable in under 30 seconds without trying a second case.
